old: Underneath it all is the image of someone jumping toward you — not gently.
It comes from a word meaning 'to jump at' — the sense of sudden, forceful approach.
Its close cousin, meaning much the same thing, is 'assail' — both trace back to the same Old French verb.
clues: This word for a violent act, used as both noun and verb, traces back to Latin words meaning 'toward' and 'jump,' so at heart it is a leap at someone.
It means a sudden, forceful attack on a person or a stronghold, more serious than a scuffle, and in law it names a specific crime against a person.
A close cousin of assail, it completes the legal phrase '___ and battery,' and a blaring, garish spectacle can be called an ___ on the senses.
